matches.rule: NAMED, NOT UPHELD — the mechanical rule never proposed this one and could not. `namesake.choose` weighs the FIRST forename token, and the register prints this man's MIDDLE name in the forename's place, so GURTREY was put to all the Blanchards the town holds and named none of them. What names him is the town's own directory: Fergus 1843 prints 'Blanchard, Francis Gurtrey, capitalist, res 45 Wells [died, Brooklyn, N.Y., 1872.]' — forename Francis, middle name Gurtrey — and Fergus 1839 and Norris 1844 print the same man 'Francis G.' GURTREY is that middle name, and the card carries it as Gantry because the poll of 1834 prints him 'Blanchard, F. Gantry'. THE REGISTER PROVES ITS OWN HABIT HERE, AT ONE SALE. The six GURTREY rows (purchase nos 0367525-0367530, volume 817 page 027) and the three F G rows (0376893-0376895, volume 818 page 010) are the SAME school section — section 16, T39N R14E, type SC — entered on 22 and 24 October 1833, the days the school section was sold off by lot and by block. One buyer, one auction, two volumes of the register, two renderings of one name; the domain's README already records this habit under T-0990, where HUNTER E E and HUNTER EDWARD E are the same 80 acres of section 13 on the same day at the same price. WHAT IS NOT NAMED BY IT. The town's other documented Blanchard is W. G. Blanchard, the house-and-land agent of the Democrat of 9 July 1834, and his forename initial is W: he is refused on the same ground the crosswalk refuses him against every other Blanchard reading. Joseph Blanchard the blacksmith is a man of the directories and not an 1835 resident. Nothing reached prints a second Gurtrey Blanchard anywhere. AND IT IS STILL A PURCHASE. The Residence column reads UNKNOWN on all six rows, so this names a buyer and never an occupant, and it places nobody on that ground. The six rows are lot 1 of block 2, block 21, lot 8 of block 141, block 3, lot 7 of block 82 and lot 1 of block 141 of the school section, $547.00 in all (ls0076-ls0081). Two of them state a price per acre of 3.69 against 0000.00 acres, which is the acreage of the F G row ls0074 standing in the wrong column of the deposit; it is carried as the register has it and read as no acreage at all.

matches.rule: BRONSON ARTHUR matches Arthur Bronson: the forename names Arthur Bronson of the 1 person of this surname, and the forename agrees in full.

ruling.reasoning: Thirteen parcels over the three days of the school-section auction, 22-24 October 1833, and the town's own tax list of 1833 names an Arthur Bronson in the same year. The forename is doing real work in this register rather than riding on a rare surname: BRONSON FREDERIC and BRONSON FREDERICK stand beside him on other rows, and the layer holds only the Arthur. The old-settler death notices are the second document. UPHELD ON THOSE TWO ARMS AND ON NOTHING ELSE. A SENTENCE WAS STRUCK FROM THIS RULING on 14 September 2026, under the answer T-1017 records at `questions_ruled`. It had argued that “a town assessing a man and an auction of the town's own school section are the same twelve months and the same ground”, which reads the purchase as evidence of PRESENCE. It is not: a town taxes a non-resident on the ground he holds in it, and T-1017 refused exactly that inference. The buyer is also the auction's fourth largest hand, and the town's own historians print him as one of “two visitors to the settlement from New York — Charles Butler and Arthur Bronson”, who sent the Chicago Lyceum two hundred volumes “on their return home” (Moses & Kirkland, History of Chicago vol. 2, printed page 367, claim bk_mose2_021). The ruling is an IDENTITY ruling and stands: it says which Bronson the register's rows belong to, not that he lived here. What his card says about residence is a separate question, filed as T-1117.

THREE WHOLE BLOCKS FOR $1,205 AGAINST A CARD THAT IS ONE LINE OF A TAX ROLL. The register enters RUSSELL SAMUEL for blocks 90, 86 and 45 at the school-section sale of 23 and 24 October 1833, among the largest single-hand takings of that sale; the card is a G3 PROJECTED RESIDENT — the ladder's own weakest rung — documented once, on the town's tax list of 1833, and corroborated by nothing. No press printing, no poll list, no middle initial, UNKNOWN in the Residence column, `present_on_scene_date` uncertain, and no Samuel Russell printed in Fergus 1839, Fergus 1843 or Norris 1844. That is one name-only reading and nothing else, the shape cohort B refused eleven times. The rule's own words govern: a bare name on each side is refused however unlikely the coincidence looks, and here the coincidence is not even unlikely — the register's biggest buyers at that sale were not all townsmen. Refused; three blocks, 13.58 acres and $1,205.00 come back off the card. The wider question this row and SKINNER JOSEPH raise together — whether buying at the town's OWN school-section sale is itself a check on a town-side name — is filed rather than decided here, because deciding it would change rulings already made.

refusals.rule: THE CLOSEST CALL IN THE COHORT, AND THE LINE IT DRAWS IS THE ONE C3 ADDS: a second document must SAY something, not merely repeat the name. The town holds Joseph Skinner twice — the tax list of 1833 and one return of letters uncalled-for at the post office, 1 April 1834 — and NEITHER prints a trade, a street, an office or a middle initial. No directory of 1839, 1843 or 1844 prints a Joseph Skinner at all, which is the test cohort A found decided all three of its refusals, and the card's own `present_on_scene_date` is uncertain. Counting to two is not the rule; the rule is that the register's row can be CHECKED against something, and two bare names cannot check a third. What argues the other way is worth stating because it is the reason this is close: the rows are lots 1 and 8 of block 117 at the town's OWN school-section sale of 22 October 1833, and a man on the town's tax list of that same year is the kind of man who bought there. That argument is not one of the rule's four arms and it would, if admitted, reopen rulings already made — so it is FILED as a question rather than used here. Refused; two lots and $212.00 come back off the card.

The closest call in this cohort, and it goes the same way. The Democrat's letter list of 20 May 1835 prints 'Minard, Ira 2'; the register enters an Ira Minard on 161 acres in T40N R14E five weeks later, on 27 June 1835. The proximity is striking and it is not a check: the card is a letter-list identity with nothing else on it, no initial, no trade, no second document, and the residence column reads UNKNOWN on both rows. Upholding here would be upholding a coincidence of date, which is the register telling us when somebody bought, not who. One further reading naming Ira Minard in the town would carry it.

refusals.rule: THE COMMONEST SURNAME IN THE TOWN, A BARE FORENAME, AND THREE PRINTED CLAIMANTS. The register's ls0501 is SMITH GEORGE, 80 acres in section 6 T40N R14E on 27 June 1835 at $2.80 the acre, with UNKNOWN in the Residence column. The card is a coffee-house keeper, minted from the Democrat of 5 November 1834 and 20 May 1835 and holding a trade and nothing else — no street, no household, no civic roll, and `present_on_scene_date` uncertain because the corpus stops six weeks before the scene date. Against that the printed record holds at least three distinct George Smiths: Fergus 1839's “Smith, George W., general merchant, North Water street”, Fergus 1843's “Smith, George (George Smith & Co.) ... bankers and exchange brokers, 1 LaSalle”, and Norris 1844's two entries for the banking house. The layer holds ELEVEN Smiths, and the register sells to eleven spellings of the surname. A coffee-house keeper's trade predicts no quarter-section, the bare forename excludes nobody, and upholding this would put a speculator's entry on the card of the one George Smith in the town whose record contains no land at all. Refused; eighty acres and $224.00 come back off the card.

The register's ls0581 is bare JOHN MURPHY, 80 acres in section 4 T38N R14E on 4 June 1835, with no middle initial and UNKNOWN in the Residence column, and there is nothing in it that could choose between them. THE CARD IS STRONG AND THAT IS NOT THE QUESTION. This household is, in its own note's words, the best-attested occupancy of a named building in the dataset — Andreas twice, in two chapters, has Mr and Mrs John Murphy taking charge of the Exchange Coffee House in August 1834 and staying to 1836, and the polls of 1834 and 1835 hold him. All of that argues that a John Murphy lived here; none of it argues that THIS John Murphy entered those eighty acres, and a tavern keeper's trade predicts a quarter-section purchase no better than a labourer's does. What the card demonstrates is the thinness the Brown rule was written for: the layer holds one John Murphy because the layer is thin, and the town printed at least two. Refused; eighty acres and $100 come back off the card.
refusals.was_proposed_as: MURPHY JOHN matches John Murphy: the forename names John Murphy of the 3 people of this surname, and the forename agrees in full.

THE TOWN PRINTS THE FORENAME IN FULL EXACTLY ONCE, and every other reading on the card is an initial that the directory's own pages give to a different man. The card's one contemporary printing is the Democrat of 6 August 1834, “Nehemiah King”. After that it holds the Fort Dearborn Addition lot sale of June 1839, where the bidder is printed “N. King”; Norris 1844's “King, N. clerk, at T. King's”; and a Fergus 1839 line matched on the initial N which reads, in full, “King, Nathaniel, clerk, Tuthill King”. NATHANIEL IS NOT NEHEMIAH. The directory prints a Nathaniel King clerking for Tuthill King and the 1844 volume prints an N. King doing the same thing in the same shop, so the N. readings have a documented owner who is not this man, and the card is gathering them on an initial — C1's ANDREWS DAVID test, read the field and not the grade. What is left to check the register's three June 1835 rows against is one newspaper printing of a name, with no trade, no street, no office and UNKNOWN in the Residence column. That is one name-only reading and nothing else, which is the shape of eleven of cohort B's twelve refusals. Refused; filed on the way past as the card's own question.

GARRETT A ET CO is refused against A. Garrett: the register sets 'ET CO' after the name, which is the page saying the purchaser was a PARTNERSHIP, and this crosswalk proposes correspondences between a purchaser and a PERSON. The identification of the firm with A. Garrett is probably right and is not what is refused; what is refused is writing the house's entry onto his card as his own.

The town's whole record of George Hall is that somebody else repudiated a note owed to him. The Chicago Democrat of 29 July 1835 prints a caution 'against purchasing a Note, given by me to George Hall, dated June 24. 1835, for fifty dollars' — and the advertiser's own name is sheared off at the crop edge, so even the other party to it is not named. That is ONE reading, it is the ONLY thing in the corpus that names him, there is no directory line in any of the three volumes, no civic roll, no census, no trade and no street. The card's own present_on_scene_date reads `uncertain` for exactly this reason: the earliest source that names him is later than 1 July 1835. Two register rows of 27 June 1835, 160 acres, Residence UNKNOWN, against one press mention: a bare name on each side, which the rule refuses however close the dates fall. Refused, and the 160 acres come back off the card.

REFUSED against Thomas Church, and not because the man is a stranger — the directories hold him firmly enough, a grocer at 109-111 Lake through 1839, 1843 and 1844. Two things refuse it. The register writes THOS JR, and the JR is the page saying there was ANOTHER Thomas Church of the same county, presumably the father; the town holds one Thomas Church and nothing on its side distinguishes the two, so the one token that discriminates here is checked against nothing. And the town's 1835 record of him is thinner than the directories make it look: the card is written, in its own words, almost entirely to keep a building from being anonymous, its present_on_scene_date says nothing places him in the town on any particular date, and the source that names him names him as the BUILDER of the first store on Lake Street rather than as its occupant. That the identification is probably right is not what is refused. The 160 acres in section 34, T39N R13E, entered 5 August 1835, are retracted.

REFUSED, and the two initials are not the discriminator they look like. The town's whole record of an L. B. Cobb is ONE line — 'Cobb, L. B.' in the 1835 poll list — and the register's 'COBB L B' is the second bare name; the ruling rule calls that two name-only readings and not an identity. What makes the refusal positive rather than an admission of thinness is the Cobb the town DOES document, and he carries the same middle initial: S. B. Cobb, saddle, harness and trunk manufactory at the corner of Lake street, advertised in the American of 8 and 13 June 1835 out of the dissolution of Goss & Cobb, a 'Silas Cobb' in the Democrat's letter list of 1 April 1834, and 'Cobb, Silas B.' at 171 Lake in Fergus 1839 and 'Silas Bowman' in Norris 1844. Beside him the directories print one other Cobb, Geo. W., a clerk. So the B does not choose between the proposal and its namesake — both have it — and the only thing that does is the forename initial, read once on each side and printed nowhere else in the corpus. A $9,000 lot (lot 2 of block 33, 21 June 1836) is a large thing to hang on a single letter that no second document repeats. Retracted.

refusals.rule: REFUSED, and this project has already refused the identical name once. The register prints JOHN bare on all seven rows of 27 September 1830 with UNKNOWN in the Residence column, and a bare John Kinzie is the one Chicago name of 1830 that cannot be read off the layer: the printed record holds John Harris Kinzie, register of the U.S. land office, AND 'Kinzie, John Harris, jr., killed, Ft. St. Charles, Ark., June 18, 1862, a. 33' (Fergus 1843), AND the elder John Kinzie of Hubbard's own pages. T-0501 met this exact string in McIlvaine's list of the trustees elected 11 August 1834 and REFUSED it — 'the printed name is impossible for the man it looks like and ambiguous among the men it could be' — saying in terms that the identification is probable and was not that pass's to make. THE ARGUMENT THAT WOULD OVERTURN IT IS AVAILABLE AND IS NOT TAKEN, and it is recorded so a later run can weigh it rather than rediscover it: the elder died in 1828 and cannot buy in 1830, and the junior's printed age puts him at about one year old that September, so chronology leaves only John Harris. That is elimination, not a token on the page; the register supplies no middle initial, no trade and no residence, and HARMON ISAAC declined the same shape of argument for the same reason. Consistency between two domains reading one name is worth more here than seven lots. Seven rows of the first town sale and $129 retracted.

REFUSED, and the middle initial the town does hold for a George Lee is the WRONG ONE. The register enters LEE GEORGE W seven times in the June 1836 town sale, and the card it is proposed onto carries exactly three readings: the Democrat's list of letters remaining in the Post Office at Chicago on 20 May 1835, which prints 'George Lee' and nothing else about him and which the newspapers layer itself flags letter_list_only; the residents card built from it; and one St. Cyr marriage of 1 October 1835 signed 'G. S. Lee', folded on by the forename initial alone. So the only middle initial anywhere on the card reads S, against the register's W. The printed record of the surname does not repair it: Fergus 1839, Fergus 1843 and Norris 1844 between them print Benjamin Tyler, Daniel, Daniel J., David S., David Stewart, John and Thomas Lee, and no George at all, and the first city election of 2 May 1837 polls no Lee in any ward. An uncalled-for letter and a tract entry are two name-only readings and do not make an identity (the_ruling_rule), and here they do not even agree on the man's initials. NOTED FOR A LATER RUN, not acted on: whether 'G. S. Lee' belongs on this card at all is a separate question from this ruling, and refusing the purchase does not answer it.

REFUSED, on the commonest surname in the cohort and the thinnest card under it. What the town holds for a George Miller is one line of the 1833 tax list (tax_1833_073) and the residents card made from it — no trade, no address, no second reading. Against that, the surname is printed as often as any in the town and never with this forename: Fergus 1839, Fergus 1843 and Norris 1844 print Bernhart, Capt. Harry, Charles/Chas., Daniel, David, H., Henry, Jacob, John, John Newhouse, Peter, Porter, Robert, S. T. and William Miller, and the Democrat and the American between 1833 and 1835 print eighteen more readings of the surname — Chas., Col. Samuel, Daniel, F. W., Henry F., Jacob, Jacob V., Jesse, Jesse F., John, Lorin, Marshall, Matthias B., Samuel and an uncertain L. P. — with no George among them. Nor does the 1837 city poll: its only Millers are Daniel and John B. The three rows are lot 8 of block 18 and lots 5 and 6 of block 36, all entered 27 September 1830 at $25, $36 and $27 — the original sale again, and thirty-three months before the tax line. A bare name in a register and a bare name on a tax roll do not make an identity.

refusals.rule: REFUSED — the BROWN WM shape at its plainest, and the cohort's clearest case that an initial is not a forename. The register prints a single letter, J, on two lots of the June 1836 town sale (lot 3 of block 41, $1,125, and lot 8 of block 38, $1,166), and the printed record of the surname holds at least four distinct men whose forename begins with it: Jacob Miller the blacksmith of Indiana Street and Jacob V. Miller (Fergus 1843, Norris 1844, the Democrat, the old-settler death notices), Jesse F. Miller (Democrat, 19 August 1835), Jonathan Miller (St. Cyr, 1838) and John Miller, with a John Newhouse Miller and a John B. Miller besides. The mechanical rule reached miller_john only because the residents layer is thinner than the town was. That card is itself name-only in every one of its readings — poll_1833_020, tax_1833_074, poll_1834_072 and two Democrat readings, one of them a letter list — so even if the initial could be made to choose, there would be nothing on the far side to check the register against.

refusals.rule: REFUSED, and the reading that made the card look thick belongs to another town. miller_samuel carries five readings, and on the face of it two of them are newspaper readings that are not letter lists — 'Col. Samuel Miller' in the Democrat of 25 February 1834 and 'Samuel Miller' on 4 March 1834, the second carrying the occupation 'agent'. Read at the page they are ONE advertisement printed twice, David Carver's storage, commission and lumber notice, and its closing sentence is 'Calvin Britain esq. at St. Joseph, and Col. Samuel Miller, Michigan City, are his Agents, who will immediately forward any article directed to him.' The Colonel is Carver's agent at MICHIGAN CITY, Indiana — named in a Chicago paper because Chicago readers shipped through him, not because he lived here. Strip that fold and what remains for a Chicago Samuel Miller is two bare names: tax_1833_075 and an 1832 Black Hawk enrollment (blackhawk_1832_070), neither with a trade, an address or a second document. The register's four rows are lots 3, 4, 5 and 6 of block 14 entered 27 September 1830 at $20, $20, $40 and $30 — the original sale, two years before the muster. No Samuel Miller is printed in Fergus 1839, Fergus 1843 or Norris 1844. Two name-only readings do not make an identity, and a third that turns out to name an Indiana man makes it worse rather than better. The fold itself — a Michigan City agent's two readings sitting on a Chicago resident card — is filed as T-1040 rather than repaired here: a ruling refuses a purchase and does not rewrite a card.

refusals.rule: REFUSED. Amasa Wright's whole card is one line of one civic list — `civic:tax_1833_113`, 'Wright, Amasa' on the tax list of 1833 — and the identity master holds nothing else under him at all: no trade, no address, no second document. That is the STANLEY JOSEPH shape cohort B refused seven times over, and the layer itself grades him `inferred`, `projected_resident`. Every printed record that could have corroborated an A. Wright refuses the surname by name: Fergus 1843 weighs six Wrights and records that none carries the initial A, Norris 1844 weighs two and records the same, and the Second Presbyterian roll weighs eleven and records the same. The printed Wrights are Edward, John, John S./John Stephen, Timothy, Truman G., Walter, Winthrop, P. R. and Mrs. Hulda — not one A across three directories. The one 'A. Wright' anywhere in the corpus is a bidder in Fergus 1839's Fort Dearborn Addition lot sale, two lots of block 13 at $1,040, and it reaches this card by 'the given name of both begins A' — an initial-only reading supporting an initial-only purchase, which is the proposal over again rather than a check on it. The old-settler match is worse: 'Wright, Abner Mills', died 1890 aged 62-8-26, is folded on by the same A and was seven years old in 1835. And the register knows its Wrights — JOHN thirteen times, T G nine, JOHN F four, J S three, TRUMAN G twice — so a bare A is the one Wright in the book with nothing to hold on to, exactly as cohort A found WRIGHT T. One lot, lot 7 of block 5 on 28 June 1836, $900.

refusals.rule: REFUSED, and it is the cohort's one refusal. The reading is a bare forename initial with no middle initial, and the town's own PRINTED record holds two Wrights whose forename begins with T: 'Wright, Truman G., speculator, bds Tremont House' and 'Wright, Timothy, Michigan ave. cor. Madison st', both in Fergus 1839, Timothy again in Fergus 1843 boarding at Mrs. John Wright's. That is the BROWN WM rule exactly — a second printed claimant, not merely a common surname. The register makes the same point on its own account: it writes T G nine times and TRUMAN G twice, so the hand that entered this man ordinarily wrote the G, and this single row of 28 June 1836 has not got it. Both upheld spellings of Truman G. Wright rest on that middle initial and cannot lend it to a spelling that lacks it. Lot 7 of block 5, $900, is retracted from the card.
